title: The Crowd
author: Gustave Le Bon
public_title: Can a crowd be better than the people in it? | Gustave Le Bon
hook: Can a crowd make decent people worse, or sometimes better, than they would be alone?

sections.title: Two answers to one question
sections.narration: Think of the last time you were part of a crowd: a stadium, a protest, a packed train platform, a group chat that turned on someone. Did you feel more yourself, or less? Gustave Le Bon, writing in the 1890s, asked whether a crowd can be moral at all, and his first answer is blunt. He says that "it is quite evident that crowds are too impulsive and too mobile to be moral." Morality, in his sense, means steady respect for social conventions and the constant holding back of selfish impulses, and a crowd, he argues, cannot hold anything steady for long. But he does not stop there. In the very next breath he adds a twist: "crowds may exhibit at times a very lofty morality." So the same author gives two answers to one question, and the tension between them is what makes this short chapter worth reading slowly. In this video we will follow both answers, look at the examples he uses, and then ask what survives when we read him with modern eyes. Keep one thing in mind as we go: Le Bon is describing tendencies he believed he saw, not laws proven by experiment, and some of his claims have been criticised ever since.

sections.title: Why crowds get a bad name
sections.narration: Le Bon notes that the few thinkers who had studied crowds before him looked almost only at their crimes. If you study riots, lynchings and massacres, you will naturally decide that crowds are cruel. He says that conclusion is often right, but he asks why it is right. His explanation is this: "Simply because our savage, destructive instincts are the inheritance left dormant in all of us from the primitive ages." In other words, he does not think a crowd invents cruelty. He thinks it releases something that each person usually keeps locked away because acting on it alone would be dangerous. Inside a crowd, he says, the individual is assured of impunity, because nobody can point to a single person who is responsible. He even draws a line from the ferocity of a mob to the pleasure of a hunting party, many people gathering to chase one animal. You may find that comparison unfair, and you are allowed to. What is worth keeping is the mechanism he points to: when responsibility is spread across a hundred people, each of them feels a little less of it.

sections.title: The other side of the ledger
sections.narration: Now comes the part that most summaries of Le Bon skip. He insists that a crowd "may be guilty of murder, incendiarism, and every kind of crime, but it is also capable of very lofty acts of devotion, sacrifice, and disinterestedness." The examples he gives are soldiers, volunteers and believers who faced death for a cause, often one they only half understood. Appeals to glory, honour and patriotism, he says, work especially well on a person who is part of a crowd, sometimes to the point of giving up a life. Notice how double-edged this is. The same quality that lets a crowd forget its own safety also lets it be steered into disaster by a clever speaker. Le Bon does not pretend that sacrifice is automatically good. He is only pointing out that the capacity for it is real, and that an individual standing alone would be far less likely to show it. For a modern reader this is an uncomfortable idea, because history has plenty of heroic crowds and plenty of terrible ones, and sometimes they are the same crowd on different days.

sections.title: When self-interest switches off
sections.narration: Here is one of his sharpest lines. "Personal interest is very rarely a powerful motive force with crowds, while it is almost the exclusive motive of the conduct of the isolated individual." Read that twice. If it is even partly true, it flips a common assumption. We usually imagine that people act in groups for the same selfish reasons they act alone, only louder. Le Bon says the opposite: alone, we calculate; together, we follow a feeling, a phrase, an order. His example is a strike. Workers who walk out, he says, often do so more in obedience to an order than to win a small pay rise. You can test the idea against your own life. Think of a time you joined something you did not fully understand because everyone around you was committed. Did you stop asking what was in it for you? The limitation to remember is that Le Bon had very little data. He relied on history books and on observation, so this is a hypothesis to examine, not a result to accept.

sections.title: Scoundrels with principles
sections.narration: The most surprising claim in the chapter is about bad people. Le Bon writes: "Even in the case of absolute scoundrels it often happens that the mere fact of their being in a crowd endows them for the moment with very strict principles of morality." He leans on the historian Hippolyte Taine, who reported that the men who carried out the September massacres of the French Revolution handed in the wallets and jewels they had taken from their victims, instead of keeping them. Another example is the crowd that burst into the Tuileries palace in 1848 and, though ragged and hungry, did not steal the objects around it. Le Bon calls this a moralisation of the individual by the crowd, and he is careful to say it is not a constant rule, only one that he has often seen. He even points to the theatre, where a rough audience demands exaggerated virtue from the hero and murmurs at a slightly risky line. Whether these stories are accurate or tidy is a fair question. But the pattern is interesting: a group can set a standard that none of its members would set alone.

sections.title: What this does and does not prove
sections.narration: Pause here and be a careful reader. Le Bon reports that earlier writers "have come to the conclusion that the moral standard of crowds is very low", and he spends the chapter complicating that verdict. Le Bon is not a modern psychologist. He did not run studies, he held strong opinions about class and race that we now reject, and later researchers have argued that crowds are often more rational and more varied than he claims. Studies of real riots and protests find that most people in them behave in ordinary, purposeful ways, and that violence often comes from small groups. So you should not take his portrait as a scientific description of every crowd. What you can take is a set of questions that still help. When do I feel less responsible because others are present? When do I follow a feeling because the group is carrying it? When does a shared cause lift me above my usual self, and when does it excuse me from thinking? Those questions work whether or not Le Bon's examples are exact, and they do not require you to agree with his politics, which are not what this chapter is really about.

sections.title: Reasoning is not always the hero
sections.narration: The chapter ends with a thought that is easy to misread. Le Bon says we should not complain too much that crowds are guided by unconscious considerations and do not reason: "Had they, in certain cases, reasoned and consulted their immediate interests, it is possible that no civilisation would have grown up on our planet and humanity would have had no history." He is arguing that some of humanity's biggest efforts, from building cathedrals to defending cities, were driven by belief and devotion more than by calculation. You do not have to agree. A fair reply is that reasoning built plenty of civilisation too, including medicine, law and science. The useful takeaway is more modest. Notice which of your own commitments came from careful thought and which came from belonging, and give each its proper place. A good life probably needs both. As you finish this video, ask yourself one question and answer it honestly: in the last month, where did you act as part of a crowd, and would you do it the same way alone?
